issues.legal_issue: The testimony of a single eyewitness may support a conviction when the witness is reliable and apparent discrepancies are immaterial.
material_facts: A witness who was working in the field testified that she saw the accused attack the deceased.
The witness’s presence at the scene was supported by the recovery of groundnuts, shells and a gunny bag, and her account remained credible despite lengthy cross-examination.
The trial court relied on omissions and discrepancies that did not materially affect the account of the assault.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness was reliable, and her testimony could form the basis of the conviction notwithstanding the immaterial discrepancies.
issues.legal_principle: The credibility of a witness is assessed by the intrinsic quality and worth of the testimony; a reliable witness’s evidence can itself support a conviction, and immaterial omissions or discrepancies do not justify rejecting it. The Court also considered whether purported contradictions with a statement recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were material.

rule.if: criminal_trial_for_offence and eyewitness_saw_assault and eyewitness_testimony_is_reliable and discrepancies_are_immaterial

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.eyewitness_saw_assault: A witness testified that she saw the accused assault the deceased.
predicates.eyewitness_testimony_is_reliable: The witness’s presence and account were supported by the evidence, and cross-examination did not undermine her credibility.
predicates.discrepancies_are_immaterial: The omissions and differences in the witness’s account did not materially affect its substance.

issues.definition: When a reliable eyewitness saw the assault and the discrepancies in that account are immaterial, the testimony of that one witness can support a conviction in a criminal trial.

issues.legal_issue: The testimony of a prosecution witness who is declared hostile is not automatically erased and may be relied on in part if that part remains credible.
material_facts: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution’s account of the actual assault and was cross-examined by the prosecutor with the court’s permission.
The witness nevertheless gave evidence about the presence of another eyewitness, the accused appearing at the scene, and the deceased later being found bleeding.
Those portions were supported by the other eyewitness and by physical evidence recovered from the scene.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to discard the witness’s evidence altogether; the credible portions supporting the prosecution could be considered.
issues.legal_principle: Under Satpaul v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1976 SC 294, a witness’s evidence is not washed off the record merely because the witness is cross-examined by the party calling them with the court’s permission; the fact-finder may accept a credible part with due care. Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, AIR 1976 SC 202, likewise holds that such evidence remains admissible and may support a conviction if corroborated by other reliable evidence.

rule.if: criminal_trial_for_offence and prosecution_witness_declared_hostile and part_of_testimony_remains_credible and credible_part_is_corroborated

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.prosecution_witness_declared_hostile: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution’s account and was permitted to be cross-examined by the prosecutor.
predicates.part_of_testimony_remains_credible: Some of the witness’s testimony remained believable despite the witness not supporting the prosecution on the whole incident.
predicates.credible_part_is_corroborated: Other reliable evidence supported the portion of the witness’s testimony that remained credible.

issues.definition: When a prosecution witness is declared hostile, a credible part of the witness’s testimony may be relied on if other reliable evidence corroborates it.

issues.legal_issue: Insignificant discrepancies among witnesses and an unexplained time stated in the charge do not require rejection of otherwise credible evidence where the accused were not prejudiced.
material_facts: Several witnesses testified that they saw the accused carry the deceased’s severed head and take it to the village gate.
The differences identified by the trial court concerned details such as how the head was tied, who was present, and minor omissions in earlier statements.

The eyewitnesses placed the assault in the morning and the later carrying of the head around noon; the differing time in the charge was unexplained, and the record did not show that it prejudiced the accused.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies and the time stated in the charge did not justify disbelieving the witnesses or the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Witness evidence should be assessed for whether discrepancies are material to its substance, rather than rejected on account of insignificant differences or omissions. A mistaken time stated in a charge does not undermine the case where the evidence is consistent in context and no prejudice to the accused is shown.

rule.if: criminal_trial_for_offence and witnesses_describe_same_continuous_occurrence and discrepancies_are_insignificant and charge_time_error_caused_no_prejudice

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.witnesses_describe_same_continuous_occur: The witnesses’ accounts concern connected stages of the same occurrence.
predicates.discrepancies_are_insignificant: The differences concern minor details or omissions and do not undermine the substance of the witnesses’ accounts.
predicates.charge_time_error_caused_no_prejudice: The time stated in the charge differed from the evidence, but the accused were not shown to have been prejudiced by that difference.

issues.definition: When witnesses describe the same continuous occurrence, their insignificant discrepancies and a charge-time error that caused no prejudice do not invalidate otherwise credible evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution need not explain simple and minor injuries on the accused when those injuries do not outweigh substantial reliable evidence of the crime.
material_facts: The accused had one incised wound each, which the doctor described as simple and minor.
The prosecution presented multiple independent witnesses who consistently described the attack and the accused carrying the deceased’s severed head.
The deceased had suffered numerous injuries, and the record did not establish that he caused or could have caused the accused’s injuries.
issues.conclusion: The failure to explain the accused’s minor injuries did not make the prosecution case suspect.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the prosecution must explain injuries on an accused depends on the facts and circumstances. Simple, minor injuries do not outweigh consistent evidence from numerous independent witnesses, particularly where the evidence does not establish that the deceased caused those injuries.

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.accused_have_only_simple_minor_injuries: The accused’s injuries are limited and medically described as simple and minor.
predicates.multiple_independent_witnesses_give_cons: Several independent witnesses consistently describe the accused’s commission of the crime.
predicates.deceased_not_shown_to_have_caused_injuri: The evidence does not establish that the deceased caused or could have caused the accused’s injuries.

issues.definition: When the accused have only simple injuries, several independent witnesses give a consistent account, and the deceased is not shown to have caused those injuries, the prosecution’s failure to explain them does not make the case suspect.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s assessment of the evidence is perverse and unreasonable.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting eyewitness and other witness testimony on grounds that included minor discrepancies and an unexplained difference in the time of the incident.
The High Court reassessed the evidence, set aside the acquittal and convicted the accused.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s findings patently wrong and perverse and agreed that the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and the appeal against the resulting conviction was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court should be slow to interfere with an acquittal, but may do so when reassessment shows that the trial court’s approach to the evidence and its resulting findings are perverse and unreasonable.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction_after_acquitta: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction entered after an appellate court set aside an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_findings_are_perverse_and_un: The trial court rejected credible evidence on grounds that did not reasonably justify its conclusions.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed, the reversal is justified when the trial court’s findings were perverse and unreasonable.
